projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Phillip Mann was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran John Phillip Mann. Mr. Mann served in the U.S. Army Air Force, with the 20th Air Force, 313th Wing, 505th Group, 483rd Squadron. He served in the Pacific Theatre and his last rank was 1st Lieutenant. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded on July 12, 2004. John was 80 at the time of this recording. Tom Swope: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: 1941 I was living in Rolla, Missouri. I lived in Rolla. I was born in 1924. I lived in Rolla until I entered the Air Force in 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you still in school in '41 -- still in high school?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: I had just entered the first quarter at the Missouri School of Mines and Metallurgy in Rolla, which they now call the University of Missouri at Rolla. I had the first quarter but I talked to all the professors into giving me an incomplete except my father who's a professor and he insisted that I finish his course at home. And enlistments had been enclosed -- had been closed at that time, but dad's secretary was on the local draft board, so she gave me a letter which entitled me to volunteer for induction. So I went into St. Louis in December of 1942, and the recruiting stations were in the big Union Depot down there. So I went to the Army and they didn't want any part of me and thank God the Marines didn't want any part of me, and the Air Force, for some reason or other, took me. And they said why don't you come back here in three days and be sure and bring enough clothes because we're gonna keep you, and so in January I went back to St. Louis and they sent me out to Jefferson Barracks in St. Louis. And it was cold as hell down there in that Mississippi -- Mississippi River. And they were so crowded that they had four of us living in a tent with an old potbelly stove and it was 20 below zero and my lower lip split, it was so chapped. And I think we were out there probably about a month, and they finally got us into barracks and went through the Air Force training program -- 26 days -- and I came out of there a specialist. So they kept us for a while and I became a drill instructor. And they gave me the guys right off the street. So this one time I had about 150 guys and I was trying to talk to them -- "and no speak the English, no speak of the English" -- so I said okay guys, we don't go to the mess hall tonight -- "yeah, where is it?" That fix that. Well, I was there for awhile and I met another one of the guys was a -- had become a drill instructor, his name was Charles Smithers, and he eventually became my brother-in-law. So they sent us over to the shipping place several times. We went over as supernumeraries, which would say if something -- for some reason or other some guy couldn't come, why they would chose somebody else. So we finally got our share. The guys that were ahead of us went to the Airborne engineers. Thank God I didn't get into that mess. But they sent a bunch of us out to Fresno, California, which was the -- a holding pen for the 4th Air Force. And I finally got a call from the bomber squadron up in Portland, Oregon, B-25 Bomber Squadron. They needed a clerk typist. Well, my two attributes were a little bit of typing in a course in high school, or I could do a pretty good milk shake or a soda jerk -- I was a soda jerk, anyhow. So I went up to Portland, Oregon and that must have been probably February or March of 1943, the 42nd Bomb Squadron -- Bomb Group. The 43rd Bomb Group, I guess 42nd Bomb Squadron, B-25s, and they put me in what they call the S-2 Department, which is a squadron intelligence department. And the 1st Sergeant of that group and I couldn't stand each other. He was Sergeant Priceup(ph) from Alabama, and -- but the captain who ran the S-2 Department, he and I got along great. One of the main reasons was it that every noon we go out and play volley-ball and his guys were getting the hell beat out of them up until I came. When I came there I rammed the volley-ball down the other guys throats. So we became good buddies. And after a while he said, "hey, Air Force cadets are opening up, would you like to try for it?" And I said well I don't know -- sure I would. By that time I had become a corporal and the sergeant is laughing at me, "hey you gonna be a Air Force pilot -- ha ha ha," I was thinking to myself, yea you SOB, wait till I see you with my commission; it's gonna be hand salute, hand salute. So they sent me down to Fresno, California to take the test, and I was accepted. I went back to Fresno -- Portland. Of course I flew down there in the back end of a B-25, and you look back in the back and it starts rotating, rotating. I got as sick as a dog, threw up all over everything. When they landed in Fresno, the crew chef came around to lower the door to get me out -- guess what he got in his face. So they knew better than to put me in the back to go back to Fresno. I flew back in the nose of a B-25 -- just a beautiful ride. And we got up close to Oregon and he hedge hopped right over the top of Crater Lake. Just a beautiful sight. So they packed me up and gave me fare to Buckley Field in Denver, Colorado. And I took a nice train trip, most of it at nighttime, and Buckley Field -- you know, Portland is sea level, and of course Denver is 5,000 feet up -- I think I weighed about 225, something like that -- they have us out there running the obstacle course, and you vomit, everything else, and you keep on going. Well, a buddy and I were running this one day and we came to the place were there was this puddle of water we were suppose to jump. Well, he didn't make it over, and so he's laying there, the instructor came up and said, "what's wrong here?" And I said, well, my buddy fell down and I don't know whether he's got a broken leg or not. And the instructor said, "well, don't just lay there, do push-ups." Joke. Well, from Buckley Field went to what they call a college training detachment in Hastings, Nebraska at Hastings College. And there they gave a lot of guys what would be the equivalent of the freshman course in college, and we had 10-15 hours of flight time in Ironicas (ph) and Piper Cubs. Well, we got up there, and the instructor say, "Okay men, pull the nose up. Pull the nose down. Lift the wing up. What are you doing up there? Are you flying or gawking?" And I just loved to look up there. So this one time he said, "okay, let's take it back in." And I thought we were gonna take it back in and taxi-up and get out. We got down on the runway and he said, "okay, take it off again." So there's a -- there's a trim tab device that you have to wind to set it for landing or to take off. Well, I set if for landing. So we're going down full throttle down the runway and it wouldn't take off. It would lift up and back down, lift up, back down. He pointed to the thing and I wound that up and zoom, right up. Got back down he says, "you know, you're the only guy that I ever saw that try to combine basketball and flying." So we went from there to preflight at Santa -- at Santa Ana, California, which is I suppose 40 miles south of Los Angeles, and we got out there doing all kinds of exercises, a lot more schooling and whatnot. I think we were there probably until March or April, and then we were sent to Hondo, Texas for navigational schooling. The first, I think, five missions were about 1,000 feet over hot Texas land, and there would be three of us student navigators in there and the airplane just stunk to high heaven because everybody -- we get sick, and I thought that was going to wash us out. But that was kind of a break-in. So all the later flights were at a higher altitude and we're good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where you classified as a navigator at Santa Ana then or?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: At Santa Ana we went through this line and they were briefing us, and "what do you want to be? An airline pilot, pilot, pilot." Came to me, "navigator, pilot, pilot -- wait a minute. Come back here." They want to know "why do you want to be a navigator for?" I said well, I love geography. I love looking around. I like mathematics. I want to be a navigator. Most navigators were washed out pilots or bombardiers. So I went on to the navigation school and I was happy about it. And we were commissioned. I was commissioned a 2nd Lieutenant. A lot of the other guys were commissioned flight officers, like a warrant officer; they weren't actually a commissioned officer. Anyhow, they sent a bunch of us to Boca Raton, Florida, for radar navigation school. And that was I think about two months. Oh, in the meantime back in Fresno, California, my friend Charles Smithers had gone out there also. I looked up on a bookcase shelf, I said, "my, you got a beautiful girlfriend." "That's not my girlfriend, that's my sister." So I said, "you think she'll let me write her?" And I did, I started writing her. After we got through Boca Raton, Florida, they gave us a leave of a -- where we could go back to the next station and take as long as we needed to go -- a delay in route, I guess they call it. Well, Boca Raton they had buses that were a bunch of steps on the back of a truck. This one day I started to get on the truck. The truck started up, well, I somersaulted and skinned my leg all up. I wanted to try to get out of physical training. Well, the medic’s guy said, "na. You're okay. You can go take your training." Well, I figured the hell with them, I'm not going to do it, so I didn't. Well that got me called in to the commanding officer under the 5th Article of War and he said, "guess what John?" -- and he was -- "guess what" -- he was talking to the secretary, said this is one of these perennial goof-offs, we have to show him. So he restricted me to the Boca Raton Country Club for a week. There only five bars there and I don't know how many restaurants. And so instead of going out, we brought the gals -- people came to see us, and we had a good time. My buddy and I was up in West Palm Beach, I think, and he had a girlfriend that night and I didn't, but he rented a brand new convertible. I think it was a Ford convertible. So we were up there driving around, I was driving. And the people on the street were so friendly. They waiving to us and whistling and everything. Finally I realized I was going down the street the wrong direction -- one way street. So my buddy says, turn on this ally here. I turned in and there was a big steel telephone pool right in the middle of it and I creamed that little car. He had to take it back to them, not me. Well anyhow, after Boca Raton I went to Red Oak, Virginia. I was going to go to Lincoln, Nebraska. I went through Red Oak, Virginia where Charles Smithers was from and where his sister was, and I stayed there for about a week and we became engaged. And then I went on to Lincoln, Nebraska, and our B-29 crew was formed there and they trained -- took us by train down to Alamogordo, New Mexico where the atomic bomb later was set off. And so we started flying transition missions in the B-29 until the crew learned all the positions and everything. While we were out there I kept writing to my wife, Ann, and we decided we were going to get married. So she came out there. She never been away from Red Oak, Virginia in her life. And for her to come out there, she got a big Hee Haw, because I was 20 years-old, she was 21 and I had to get my parent's permission to get a marriage license out there but my mom wouldn't sign, but my dad said, "if he's old enough to fight, he's old enough to get married." So, so, so, and we went from Alamogordo -- we got married in Alamogordo, drove down to El Paso in my buddy's car again. Crossed our way into Juarez, Mexico. "Come in lieutenant look around. This won't cost you anything." Oh yeah. So they sent the crew by train to Kearney, Nebraska. Some of the gals, including my wife, drove up there from Alamogordo and we got to Kearney and they checked us out some more and they assigned us a brand new B-29 to fly it over to Marianas Islands to Tinian. So we bid our wives adieu and took off. And we -- I think we landed to Sacramento and packed up more gas and everything and took off to Hawaii. And going over the Golden Gate Bridge the pilot said, "navigator, give me a heading." And I walked in the very front of the airplane and pointed like Columbus and said, "follow me." So I learned later on that it wasn't my expert navigation that got us over there, because there were radio bolts up there that the pilot followed. So we landed on Hawaii and stayed there for a little while and then --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About when was that crossing?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Excuse me?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you take that flight, approximately?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Oh, that was probably late -- the very late March of 1944.

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yes. We were sent over there as one of the first replacement crews for B-29 squadrons. And we got there whatever the time was, there was Easter over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: So we took off from Hawaii and Waikiki Beach what a, what a disappointment that was and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why's that?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: I don't know. It just didn't fit what I thought it would be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not like postcards or the newsreels?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: No. None of the dancing girls. So we took off and we landed on the way over at Kwajalein Atoll, which is an island, I bet that thing is not more than 50 feet off the water. And we took off from there and landed on Tinian. And Tinian had four parallel airstrips that were, I think, 10- or 12,000 feet long, and we flew this brand new B-29 over there and we said, "oh man, this is great. We got our own plane, own airplane." Hell, we weren't even on the ground over there when somebody else got it. Well, it came time for us to have our first mission and during this time they were firebombing Japanese cities. And our luck would have it our first target was Tokyo. Well, they had a ruling, if something's wrong with your airplane and you can't get it going with everybody else, if you can get it going within an hour that everybody else takes off, you have to go. So it was our luck we got it fixed before the hour was up and we took off and got up over Tokyo. And they knew exactly where our route was and our elevation and everything. These huge thermals, what were fires -- just like a big thundercloud. Well we flew into the thermal over the fire and zip 3,000 feet up and then over the top of it and guess what happens on the other side and zip 3,000 feet down and I'm not over that yet. Well, they did hit us. They hit the whole back end of the airplane and blew the hell out of it. One guy got half of his -- the calf of the leg blown away and he's yelling, "I'm hit. Get out of here, get me out of this place." And we went on over and dropped our bombs and then took a heading back towards Tinian. And the copilot at that time got up and went back to help all the guys in the back end that got hit. So we -- there were two controls systems in a B-29. One of those got damaged and was not useable, but we almost crashed landed that thing on Iwo Jima on a Japanese pilot strip in a rainstorm. And it's sliding down the runway, almost sideways, and it stopped just before it got to a bank. And the radio comes on and we're advised by the commanding general that the island had not been secured, to get that thing the hell off of here. Well, how do you do that? You don't. 'Cause the thing was scrapped right there on the island. And that general was the Marine Corp General Howling Mad Smith. So we bummed a ride back to Tinian somewhere or other, and then they assigned us another airplane that had a big picture on the side of it of a priest and these shrubs and the name of that airplane was "Padre and His Angels." So we flew that thing nine or ten times, and we never had gasoline enough to get back from our target to Tinian. So we had to land on Iwo Jima and gas up again. Well the hierarchy is the -- I was in a group, the 483rd Group or the 505th Bomb Group and its 313 Wing. Well, they -- they thought we were goofing-off so much that they sent a wing flight engineer with us on several flights. Well, they landed that airplane one time and they tore the engines apart and found out that half of the engines were dead. So of course you don't get anywhere. Well, the winds over Japan anyhow can reach 200 knots and the B-29 is a -- cruising speed is 190, I think. Well, incidentally the four parallel runways on Tinian, if you were going towards the east for takeoff, they slop up a a little bit, and she got that airplane loaded, so total weight is 140,000 pounds. You're going uphill a little bit. And before you get off the ground you see 140 miles an hour, and the navigator sitting there fidgeting like hell. The east end of that runway was about 100 feet off the ocean and you watched the guy ahead of you take off and you see him get off the ground little bit and then they disappear over that bank because then they could go down and get a little bit of airspeed going up -- so so so. Well, the Navy had us start dropping a lot of mines for them. We bombed several targets, and one target the Japanese fighters flew right square at us. I was looking at my window and they threw fossil bombs out and splattered all over my window. Anyhow, the mining missions for the Navy, we go up and drop these magnetic or different kinds of mines. So we boxed in the inland sea so the Japanese couldn't get out of there. And then we started mining the rivers. And we really really boxed them in so they couldn't get anywhere with their shipping. Well, one of our missions we were supposed to lay mines in the Straits of Yawata, and that's the -- Yawata is the Japanese big steel making area. And on radar if you are -- radar is pointing towards a water, you see the difference between land and water. Well, if you're flying towards hills, mountains, it looks the same way. So we were looking at the radar. And it kept looking like we're supposed to be over land, over land, and it finally became so long that I told the -- there were two of us radar navigators on. I just happen to be the primary navigator -- we're both equally qualified. When the back end -- I told the guy to turn the scope up to 100 miles, and holy mackerel -- we were way off course. We're over the biggest naval base that Japan has -- Sasebo. So we dumped our mines and got the hell out of there, quick -- no anti-aircraft, no search lights, no nothing. Well after we landed, there's an invasion being prepared and they got all over us. "Where did you drop those mines over there?" Because if they were going to go over that harbor, they had to know where they were. As best we could, we told them. I almost got court-martialed over that. Thank God I wasn't. But then we were approaching time for the invasion and our airplane commander volunteered us for elite crew school for an invasion bunch. Well, they were gonna have us in B-29s fly treetop level over targets and drop 55 gallon drums of naphthalene on them. And our target was Yokohama. And thank God they dropped the atomic bombs, 'cause otherwise it would have been good-bye Charlie. We'd never made it back from that kind of a mission. So the atomic bombs were dropped and armistice came along. Then the people started coming out from the states to get in their overseas time so that you get the extra ribbon, you know. So they said, "okay, you guys got to start wearing neckties and you got to have training missions," and all this kind of crap. Well, then they started rotating people home like, depending how long of a service you had, so many points. All the good mechanics rotated back and they started sending inline mechanics, supervisors, to maintain radios and engines. We lost a couple of airplanes on just training missions. And I said the hell with that. They missed shooting me up there, so I'm not going to fly any more. Well, one of my drinking bud -- well, one of my friends was the group flight surgeon, and he said, "you crazy idiot. They're gonna court-martial you." He said, "I'm hereby grounding you for an acute anxiety reaction." Well, after that time I didn't have to fly any more, but the position of squadron adjutant became open. So I applied for that and I got it. And I started rooting around in the Articles of War and stuff, and this one day the wing commander, colonel, walks in and says, "where the hell is your safe in here?" And I said, "it's over there in the corner." "Is it chained to the floor?" And I said, "nope." Said, "I'll be back in here in an hour and I want to see that thing chained to the frame of this Quonset hut." What had happened, some of the safes in other places had been stolen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The whole thing?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: So that -- that occurred. Well any -- anyhow the Article of War -- somebody came in one day and asked if I could help him get him a dependency discharge. Well, I looked it up and saw what you had to do, the things his people had to do. Low and behold he got a dependency discharge. So everybody else heard about that, then they started -- so many of them coming around and so many of them got dependency discharges -- here comes the wing boys again. What the hell is going on down here anyhow? Well I just read what these guys needed to do out of the Articles of War-- so so so. Well, they were putting together makeup crews to fly back home, fly B-29s back. I didn't want to do that. Why should I get messed up with that again. So I waited for a boat trip home. And when it came time for me to wait for a boat, they put me on a LST or something or other with a bunch of other guys to go five miles to Tinian -- to Saipan. Saipan was that close and you could look over Saipan Harbor and you just couldn't believe the amount of vessels over there, the big aircraft carriers, the big battleships, everything. So we got over there. I guess we were there maybe a couple of weeks. I went into the NCO Club over there. The biggest bar I've ever saw in my life. The guy had a big sign there, "any kind of beer you want, I got." Well ha ha ha, I'm from St. Louis and Anheiser Bush and there's another beer out there that I like, High Park taste just like Miller High Life. So I said I'll have a High Park. He reached down under -- could have choked me, here it was. So is that so. So they put us on a baby flattop to come home, and that thing was just like a cork out there in the water. And on the way back we hadn't reached as far as Hawaii and we went through the edge of a typhoon. I was looking out the door, I said, "my, what big gray clouds out there." Gray clouds my foot, they're 40 foot high waves. So we all got sick. And I had a sebaceous cyst over my eye about the size of your knuckle. And it just so happened that on the boat were a whole bunch of flight surgeons. So they all wanted to operate on that thing and I wouldn't let them but whatever. So we got back to Long Beach, California, I guess, and got processed, and they made a recruit train to go back to St. Louis, and they assigned me as train commander. And that's fine until we got to Kansas City and about half the train evaporated. We got back to St. Louis to Justin Barracks and I said, "what the hell am I going to do? These guys took off. What am I going to do?" He said, "oh, don't worry about it, they'll be back." So I got discharged. And I thought well, you know, if something happens again, it would be nice to keep my commission. I had become a 1st Lieutenant. So I signed up for the Air Force Reserves. Well, don't you know along came the Korean War and they needed B-29 crews. So I got called up and sent to camp Kearney, New Jersey. I was up there for a week, I guess. Well, the guy who was a sales manager for a company that I was working for headed up the Cleveland Air Force Reserve. So he went to work and got me deferment up there. The other guys had to go to the Korean War. I got back here and said, "man, I didn't mean that." Then as soon as I could, I got out of the reserves and that's the end of my career.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let's back track a bit. Naphthalene, is that like Napalm?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Flammable stuff that they were dropping?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So most of your missions over Japan, were they firebombing -- well, I guess you did say you dropped mines but --

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Most of our missions were mines.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were mines -- were dropping mines?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: I think our crew got in 25 missions before they sent us to elite crew school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum. So you flew 25 missions?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other particularly memorable missions?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yes. We were flying a daytime -- daytime mission, it was going to be a full mission mission, 500 airplanes. As we got closer to Japan, we ran into this warm front and they -- we should be going up up up and we finally got up to about 25,000 feet, they said, "we can't keep the squadron; everybody for themselves." Well, 500 airplanes up there in that kind of soup. And I was looking over toward the copilot, and all of a sudden I saw him yank the wheel away from the pilot and switch it up. And out the window there, what do you think I saw? "Padre and His Angels." And that's the closest to heaven I'm ever gonna come. Another mission we were flying daylight missions over Osaka. And they used to base a stripped down B-29 on Iwo Jima, and there was a B-51 bunch there, and the 29 would take the B-51s up to Japan and would circle off coast until these guys came back. Well, our gunner started shooting at this airplane coming right at us -- Osaka, he was coming around a big cloud of smoke -- Holy Mackerel, don't you know it was a B-51. Thank God they missed him. Another day, most of our missions we took off at nighttime, and we got up pretty close up to Japan and daylight -- the biggest armada of boats I ever saw. One of the -- one of the -- somebody's battle group, from horizon to horizon everything you could think of. I think they were going toward Okinawa or somewhere over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now on missions, did you have any lucky charms or anything you took along?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yes I did. I had the -- the Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want. I had a ribbon like that and I carried that in my pocket. And not too long ago my granddaughter signed up for the Ohio National Guard and they said, "hey Angie, guess what," they sent her out to Fort Leavenworth, Missouri, forty miles from where I was born and raised, and they made her into an MP. They sent her down to Washington DC for a year and then they let her out for awhile and she and her former fiance volunteered to go to Iraq. So they were over in Baghdad for almost a year and she came home. And I had given her that ribbon to take over there with her. Thought it was good luck for her too. You may have read in the news where a couple of guys over there were out on a boat mission one night and they drowned. The sergeant had all his armor on and he fell in the water and the other guy jumped in to try to get him. Well they -- they were friends of hers. And she turned 22 over there. And what a way for a young gal to get broken in. And she hasn't been able to get near college yet. She -- I think signed up for six years. So she's probably got another two and a half, three years that she could be called up again. But when their group got back over here, the commanding general said, "okay. You guys have served twice, down in Washington DC and over there, so you don't go in again." Oh, yeah, tell me about it. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have much of -- getting back to World War II -- much fire opposition?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: No, not very much. Not very much at all. Just one time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: One time we were flying on that mission were we got loss -- didn't get loss -- we went to -- didn't go to the right place. Our gunners were calling in night fighters. They thought they saw night fighters out there. They weren't night fighters. We were flying down a valley and didn't know it and these were lights of buildings on site. We got medals. I got air medal with two clusters, I think, and a distinguish flying cross and those were just really if you went so many missions it was an automatic given to you but that's all right they look nice on you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about what were they called Baca bombs? Were those those little kamikazes?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have to deal with any of those?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: That's what they -- night --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's what they thought they saw?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yea.

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Have any particularly close buddies on your crew?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yes, everybody liked our bombardier. He was named Alexander Turnertopping(ph), everybody called him Top. And about a year ago I thought I'd try to see if I could round any of them up. Well, I found out that Top is living down in Anthems, Ohio. He runs a tool and die company down there. And the copilot is out in Los Angeles and is an architect. And I could not find the airplane commander and the radio operator, couldn't find, and the flight engineer had passed away, and the other navigator was up in New England -- in New York somewhere, and he said that he worked here in Cleveland for a long time, for the steel company. What was it before LTV? Not Rosen. Doesn't -- doesn't matter. But he was here for a long time working for that company and we never knew that. So none of us have ever -- ever gotten together, no. Matter of fact I been trying to find a B-29 reunion somewhere and I have not been successful in my meager trying.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: I got -- talked to the mayor, former Mayor of Parma Heights, Paul Cassidy. I had found out that he had been a B-17 navigator over in Europe and he was in the -- getting his magazine some or other and he thought maybe there be some listing of B-29 reunions in there, but not so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're talking about a B-29 reunion as opposed to a specific group or squadron?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yes, if -- if it could have been narrowed down to a squadron, that would be good, but it didn't. Well, the first night that we got over there they assigned us to a Quonset hut, and I think there were two crews, the commissioned officers, in a Quonset hut. The other guys didn't come back. They've been over on a fire bomb mission and they got shot down. So welcome to the war, boys.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your crew survived? You didn't lose anybody during the war?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: No, no, that one time is the only time we got hit bad.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was the first one?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: The first mission.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: And we had thought gee, I'm glad we are out in the Pacific, 'cause you know, those German anti-aircraft people are really accurate. Well, they were accurate enough for us, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So how about mail call? Did you get much in the way of letters or packages or anything from your wife?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Oh yeah. She sent me stuff all the time. And I didn't like pistachio nuts and she didn't know that and there was some guy over there that went ape over pistachio nuts. I don't know how you even -- how you eat those things. Do you take a handful of them and spit the shells out or what or something. But she would send me these little rum cakes and that was nice. Oh, there were Navy groups and there were Sea Bees on Tinian Island and the Sea Bees liked to go for airplane rides. And so we took one group over and they'd invite us down for steak dinners and they would trade us a case of beer for whiskey. We were allotted a 5th of whiskey a week for a buck and a quarter, and when we got low they would send another B-29 back to Tinian -- back to Hawaii for another load. Anyhow, we trade those guys whiskey for beer. And when they unloaded the boats, I'm sure it was our beer, one case for you and one case for them. So they'd trade us our beer back. What else do you guys want? Do you want a jeep? So those -- those were fun guys. And one night at our officer's club these guys from another squadron walked in. For Christ sake. What the hell are you doing here? An enlisted man dressed up in an officer's uniform, and he was from my hometown in Rolla -- Rolla, Missouri, and I knew him, Skeeter Brenson(ph.) What in the hell are you doing in here dressed up like that? Get out of here. Somebody finds out that, you're gone. So I talked him to at least leaving. Crazy guys -- punk.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you like the B-29?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yeah, it was a good airplane.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Good airplane?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: The B-20 -- anything before that, the cabins were not pressurized so they had to wear these heavy winter suits. But the B-29 was pressurized so we didn't have to wear those suits at all. And I was surprised my friend, who's Warren Brewer(ph)I, told him that after the missions they had given us number 10 cans of turkey or chicken, bread and a whole bunch of stuff after we got away from the target, why the radio operator break out all that stuff out and give us a good feeding. And Warren said they never did that for them over in Europe. Too bad, so sad.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now you mentioned the one bit of nose art and the names of the planes. Did you have any other names on your planes?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Yeah, our particular airplane, after we were assigned one, they had an insignia showing the islands of Japan burning and the name of it was "Forever Amber". And I didn't like that. Said, you know, if they ever shoot us down, they'd kill us for sure if they see that, and -- but that was it, "Forever Amber". Matter of fact, six months or so ago there was an article in the Cleveland Plain Daily, that this guy said he'd been over on Tinian and B-29s and he was in the 483rd Squadron. My goodness, that was my squadron. So I called him up and, oh, yeah, he had pictures of "Forever Amber" and he had pictures of "Padre and His Angels." My goodness. I asked if I could have some of those, and he said yeah. And I told him, "you know, I used to be adjunct of that squadron." I haven't heard from him since. I don't know what that's all about, but I didn't know him by name over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when you got back, what was your reunion with your wife like?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Great. She met me in St. Louis and then we went out to my home in Rolla and had a good visit with my parents and people out there, and then we went back to Red Oak, Virginia to live with her mother. And when I got out of the service -- I think I told you that I weighed about 225 when I went into cadets. Well, they took me down to 185 and not a ounce of fat on me. We got down to Red Oak, Virginia and oh my, those good Virginia apple pies and all that stuff, I went up to 265. And I loved it down there. I started school -- there weren't any jobs available. So I started school in a pre-engineering course at a liberal arts school in Salem, Virginia called Roanoke College. And I got into the junior year there and I was doing -- out of a 4 point possible average I had a 3.5 average or something. I was doing good. It was a closed book school; you took your test, you didn't have any books open or anything. Well, I wanted to get into an engineering school, so I applied at MIT, Carnegie Tech, Cal Tech. None of them wanted any transfer students. Somebody said, "Well, try Case Institute in Cleveland." I never heard of Case. My father was a professor out in Missouri School of Mines. He said oh yeah, Case is a good school, that's fine. So I applied at Case. And man, they jumped on me because they flunked out so many freshmen that they needed sophomores. So we came up here and thought, after I got through schooling, that we go back down to Virginia. But we liked it here so we stayed here. Well, anyhow with my good record down at Roanoke College, I signed up for way too many courses here, and I thought open book classes, this is going to be a snap. Damn near broke my neck. The -- it wasn't long before I had to drop some courses. And I transferred in with some advance courses like psychology or some other things that some of the advanced students and I was taking, like a course on metallurgy that was ordinarily given to the seniors there. As a matter of fact, I think Warren Brewer was in that class. We didn't know each over then. So I was going to graduate in January of 1951 as a mechanical engineer. I started out -- I'm a railroad fan and I always wanted -- so I thought well, I could just hang into that. I really -- it's a good thing I didn't get in as railroad guy because I never went -- well anyhow, I switched to machine design crew -- course. And our junior year they sent us out to do some interviews for jobs. Well I went out to talk to railroads Chesapeake, Ohio, New York Central, Pierre Marquette, Erie, all had their headquarters downtown there. They had positions like student engineering training. Well, boss's son had those jobs or boss's friend's son had those. Well, there was a Pennsylvania station, original station, out at 55th and Euclid and it was headed up by Case graduate. So I went in to talk to him and we talked for a while and he said, "well John, I can't take you on as an engineer, but I can take you on as a painter." So I gave him my nicest smile and left. And I got to the door and said the hell with all of you. I'm going to go home and make myself a H.O. model railroad and I'm going to be chairman of the board, so just call me chairman.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you first got back, do you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Not at all, other than not being able to find a job.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum, you didn't have dreams?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any of that stuff?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: No. No problems.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: No, I can't think of anything -- one dear old song -- "I wanted wings 'til I got the damn ole things, now I don't want them anymore." You heard that one?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've never heard that song.

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: -- one thing you can't laugh off is that you sure rear off that I'd rather be home buster with my rear then with my cluster buster. I wanted wings until I got the damn ole things, now I don't want them anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You don't remember who did that, do you?

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's great. Well, we got it.

sp.speaker: John Phillip Mann
sp.p: Well, I heard that one from my bombardier. That was an old drinking song.
